_readme: G5 hostile submissions. Each one attempts a specific escape named in docs/PRD.md 7.3.
Two things must hold for every case: it degrades to a CLEAN verdict (never IE, never a
crashed worker), and the host is left healthy with docker ps -a back at its baseline.
Any fixture printing a line starting with ESCAPED has defeated the sandbox. The suite
greps for that string, because a wrong verdict is a bug but an escape is a breach.
If this gate fails, all other work stops (docs/KICKOFF.md Phase 2).
Containment is enforced by the CONTAINER FLAGS, which are language-agnostic, so these
cases are not per-runtime for their own sake. They exist because each runtime reaches
the kernel by a different path — raw BSD sockets in C++, Go's own network poller, libuv
in Node — and a flag that failed to apply would surface in one of them first. Proving
the boundary once in Python does not prove the boundary a C++ submission sees.

cases.why: --network=none removes the interface entirely; there is nothing to connect to.
--pids-limit caps the process table long before the host notices.
--memory with --memory-swap equal means the allocation cannot be swapped out either.
Reads the CONTAINER's /etc/passwd, which is inert. The host's must be unreachable.
--read-only rootfs plus a read-only /work mount; only the tmpfs is writable.
The in-container wall-clock kill fires; --cpus keeps it from starving the host.
Output is capped and the container killed, so the worker cannot be OOMed by a firehose.
Raw BSD sockets — the lowest-level reach of any runtime here, so the first to notice if --network=none were not applied.
Go's net.Dial. The Go runtime manages its own poller, so its failure path differs from libc's.
Node's net module over libuv, a third distinct path to the same absent interface.
--read-only rootfs. Nothing outside the size-capped tmpfs is writable.
Same rootfs guarantee, reached through Go's os package rather than libc.
Same rootfs guarantee, reached through Node's fs.

T4. /out is the one mount that is genuinely WRITABLE — the driver returns results through it, and the submission runs as the same uid. The four write-outside-tmp cases all probe read-only paths, so they proved the rootfs and never touched this. --ulimit fsize bounds one file; the host-side directory watchdog bounds their sum, because RLIMIT_FSIZE does not.
